title: Robert Kraft Says Ed Sheeran Is Donating $2 Million to ‘Fight This Humanitarian Crisis’ in Gaza, and Kraft Is Matching Him: ‘All Lives Are Worth Protecting’
description: In the latest chapter of the ongoing Ed Sheeran–Macklemore–Robert Kraft situation, Sheeran and Kraft have apparently seen and raised Macklemore’s $1
body:
In the latest chapter of the ongoing Ed Sheeran–Macklemore–Robert Kraft situation, Sheeran and Kraft have apparently seen and raised Macklemore’s $1 million donation to Palestinian relief by donating $2 million each — although it’s unclear exactly to whom.

	In a statement released on the Gilette Stadium X account, Kraft said, “Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis,” but the specifics stop there. Reps for Kraft and Sheeran did not immediately respond to Variety’s request for more specific information.
	

	Kraft’s statement reads in full: “I have dedicated much of my life to building bridges between all people. I believe deeply that all lives are worth protecting. Earlier today, before Macklemore challenged me to match his donation, Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis. Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges.


	“In addition, I’d like the people who are speaking in support of the Palestinian people to know that for decades, I have supported efforts that create opportunity for Palestinians and have brought young Palestinians and Israelis together to build businesses, create jobs, and forge relationships.”

	Earlier on Wednesday, Macklemore announced that he’ll be donating the $1 million in net earnings he received from supporting Ed Sheeran on his Loop Tour to organizations working to support the Palestinian people, and invited billionaire Kraft to match his donation.
	

	The rapper was dropped from Sheeran’s current tour earlier this week after saying “free Palestine” on stage and delivering a political speech at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey at the beginning of September. He appeared to place the blame on New England Patriots owner Kraft, saying that the mogul had rallied other stadium owners to refuse to allow him to perform at their venues.

	Variety will have more on the situation as it develops.

schema.headline: Robert Kraft Says Ed Sheeran Is Donating $2 Million to ‘Fight This Humanitarian Crisis’ in Gaza, and Kraft Is Matching Him: ‘All Lives Are Worth Protecting’

title: Music Distribution, Explained: And Why It Matters More Than Ever for Independent Artists
description:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	The music
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	The music industry has never had fewer gatekeepers.

	Independent artists are increasingly releasing music without traditional label deals, while established acts have more options for retaining ownership and control over their recordings. In 2025, more than a third of artists who generated at least $10,000 in Spotify royalties were DIY artists — meaning they self-released through independent distributors — or had started their careers that way, according to Spotify. Roughly half of the royalties the service paid to the music industry last year were generated by independent artists and labels.
	

	That shift has made understanding music distribution increasingly important. More than 100,000 new recordings were delivered to digital service providers every day in 2025, according to Luminate, up 7% from the previous year, with the growth largely coming from outside the major-label distribution system. At the same time, streaming remains the engine of the U.S. recorded-music business, generating $9.47 billion in 2025.


	In other words: Artists have more ability than ever to put out music themselves, but doing so means taking on some of the business mechanics once handled largely behind the scenes by labels.The key piece of that infrastructure is the music distributor.

	In the physical era, distribution largely meant pressing records and CDs, shipping them to retailers and getting them onto store shelves. Today, digital distributors act as the bridge between an artist and Spotify, Apple Music, Amazon Music, YouTube Music, TikTok and other platforms.

	Artists have a growing number of distribution platforms to choose from, including DistroKid. While companies differ in how they charge and the services they layer around basic distribution, DistroKid uses an annual subscription model and allows artists to upload multiple releases for distribution across major digital services. All plans, which start at $24.99/year, include unlimited music uploads and royalty-splitting tools, while higher tiers add features such as customizable release dates, daily streaming statistics and support for multiple artists – all while not taking a percentage of the earnings that streaming services and stores send for an artist’s music.
	

	Once music is live, distributors also help collect recording revenue reported by streaming services and stores and make that money available to the artist or other master-rights holder. That is separate from music publishing: royalties generated by the underlying composition can travel through publishers, performing-rights organizations and other collection systems.

	For an artist choosing a distributor, the questions are therefore increasingly consequential. Which services and territories does it reach? Does it charge annually, per release or take a percentage of revenue? How does it handle collaborator splits, metadata corrections, release scheduling and payouts? And what happens to an artist’s catalog if a subscription lapses or the artist later changes distributors?Timing is another consideration. Uploading a song does not mean it appears instantly everywhere, and different services can require different processing windows. Distribution increasingly sits near the beginning of a release rollout rather than functioning as a tacked-on last step.

	None of this means distribution itself creates a hit. It doesn’t guarantee streams, playlist placement or an audience. If anything, the explosion in releases has made discovery more competitive: Luminate counted an average of 106,000 recordings arriving at digital platforms every day last year.

	But the same system has also made it possible for far more artists to reach a global audience without first securing a conventional record deal. As the line between “independent” and mainstream artists continues to blur, knowing how music actually gets from the studio to Spotify — and who controls the money and rights along the way — has become more important than ever.

schema.headline: Music Distribution, Explained: And Why It Matters More Than Ever for Independent Artists

title: How to Stream ESPN on Sling: Watch ‘Monday Night Football,’ College Football and More for $19.99 a Month
description:

	Just as t
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Just as the fall sports calendar starts heating up, watching ESPN directly is about to get a little more expensive.

	Beginning Sept. 17, ESPN is raising the price of its standalone ESPN Unlimited plan from $29.99 to $31.99 per month, while its annual subscription jumps from $299.99 to $319.99. The lower-cost ESPN Select tier is also increasing from $12.99 to $13.99 per month and from $129.99 to $139.99 annually.


	For sports fans primarily interested in ESPN’s flagship channels, however, Sling TV offers a cheaper route. The streamer’s recently launched Sling Essentials package costs $19.99 per month and includes both ESPN and ESPN2 alongside more than 10 other channels, including Disney Channel, Freeform and Hallmark Mystery. Subscribers also get 50 hours of DVR storage.
	

	For fans who want even more college sports, Sling also offers Sling Select with Sports Extra and a Season Pass option, which bundle in channels such as ESPNU, SEC Network, ACC Network and more for broader access throughout the college football season.

	Sling Essentials particularly timely with football season underway. ESPN remains the home of “Monday Night Football,” with the New York Giants taking on the Los Angeles Rams on Sept. 21 at 8:15 p.m. ET, followed by the Philadelphia Eagles and Chicago Bears on Sept. 28. ESPN2 also carries the alternate “ManningCast” for select “Monday Night Football” games.

	College football is another major draw. ESPN’s networks will carry more than 1,000 games throughout the 2026-27 season across ESPN, ESPN2, ESPNU, SEC Network, ACC Network and other platforms, in addition to the network’s weekly “College GameDay” coverage.
	

	The basic $19.99 Sling Essentials subscription gets you ESPN and ESPN2, but diehard college fans can tack on Sports Extra for an additional $11 per month, bringing the total to $30.99. The add-on brings SEC Network, ACC Network, ESPNU and ESPNEWS into the mix, giving viewers substantially more access to SEC and ACC games throughout the season.

	Baseball fans also have plenty to watch as the MLB postseason race enters its final stretch. ESPN will exclusively televise a Sept. 23 doubleheader featuring the Cleveland Guardians against the Boston Red Sox at 7 p.m. ET, followed by the Houston Astros against the Seattle Mariners at 10 p.m. ET. “Baseball Tonight” programming will surround marquee matchups with analysis and highlights.

	On the basketball front, ESPN remains one of the WNBA’s national television partners. The league returns from its FIBA World Cup break this week before concluding the regular season Sept. 24, with the playoffs tipping off Sept. 27. Disney’s ESPN and ABC networks will carry two first-round playoff series and one semifinal series.

	And ESPN’s appeal goes well beyond the games themselves. Its year-round studio slate includes “SportsCenter,” “Get Up,” “First Take,” “NFL Live,” “The Pat McAfee Show,” “Pardon the Interruption,” “College GameDay” and more, offering pregame coverage, postgame reaction, highlights, interviews and analysis throughout the week.

	Stream ESPN on Sling TV here.

schema.headline: How to Stream ESPN on Sling: Watch ‘Monday Night Football,’ College Football and More for $19.99 a Month

title: Macklemore Donating $1 Million Salary from Ed Sheeran Tour to Support Palestine: ‘I Invite Robert Kraft to Match My Donation’
description: Macklemore has announced that he’ll be donating the $1 million in net earnings he received from supporting Ed Sheeran on his Loop Tour to organizati
body:
Macklemore has announced that he’ll be donating the $1 million in net earnings he received from supporting Ed Sheeran on his Loop Tour to organizations working to support the Palestinian people, and invited billionaire Robert Kraft to match his donation.

	The rapper was dropped from Sheeran’s current tour earlier this week after saying “free Palestine” on stage and delivering a political speech at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey at the beginning of September. He appeared to place the blame on New England Patriots owner Kraft, saying that the mogul had rallied other stadium owners to refuse to allow him to perform at their venues.
	

	A rep for Kraft declined to comment on Macklemore‘s request to match the donation.


	On Wednesday, Macklemore posted another lengthy note on social media sharing that he would be donating his net earnings to organizations including Palestine Children’s Relief Fund, Heal Palestine, Gaza Soup Kitchen, Medical Aid for Palestinians, UNRWA USA National Committee and Anera.


	“With everything that has happened over the last 48 hours, I want to bring the conversation back to where it belongs: to the Palestinian people who are still being killed, still living under military occupation, and still fighting for their freedom,” he wrote. “I will be donating the entire $1 million of my net earnings from Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour to six organizations working directly to support the Palestinian people. And I invite Robert Kraft to match my donation. Whatever we disagree about, perhaps we can agree on this: Palestinian lives are worth protecting. A Palestinian life is no less valuable than any other life on this earth.”
	

	Macklemore explained that he wants to “center the parents carrying their children into hospitals without the basic resources to treat them, and the physicians, paramedics, journalists and aid workers who keep going back in. I want to center the organizers and activists who have paid real costs for standing with Palestine. Their risk is of a far different order than mine.

	“Palestinians have lived for decades without basic rights and should not have to wait another day to be free,” he continued. “That is where my focus will remain. I will continue to stand with the Palestinian people and their fight for liberation. When the news cycle moves on, which it will, don’t move with it. Free Palestine.”

	Macklemore’s latest efforts come after a tumultuous day for Sheeran, who released a statement on Tuesday morning sharing that he had nothing to do with Macklemore’s dismissal from his tour and that he preferred to remain neutral when it came to political causes. Not long after, all of the supporting acts on the Loop tour — Finneas, Aaron Rowe, Lukas Graham and Beoga — announced that they were dropping out in solidarity with Macklemore and the Palestinian people.

schema.headline: Macklemore Donating $1 Million Salary from Ed Sheeran Tour to Support Palestine: ‘I Invite Robert Kraft to Match My Donation’

title: Madonna to Open MTV Video Music Awards With First Show Performance in 23 Years
description:
Madonna is set to open the MTV Video Music Awards with her first live performance at the show in 23 years.

	The pop star last graced the VMA stage
body:
Madonna is set to open the MTV Video Music Awards with her first live performance at the show in 23 years.

	The pop star last graced the VMA stage as a performer with her iconic 2003 appearance with Britney Spears and Christina Aguilera. She already received a big look ahead of the VMAs with 11 nominations in the wake of her latest album “Confessions II,” putting her ahead of Taylor Swift with nine nominations and Ariana Grande and Sabrina Carpenter, who had seven apiece. She has 19 career wins and previously led nominations twice, with nine nods for “Vogue” in 1990 and nine for “Ray of Light” and “Frozen” in 1998.
	

	Madonna is riding high on “Confessions II,” a sequel to her 2005 dance record “Confessions on a Dance Floor.” The critically acclaimed record, her first in seven years, debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 134,000 equivalent album units and delivered her best streaming week ever. Fans are already speculating that Madonna could be a strong contender at the Grammy Awards next year, particularly in the dance and electronic categories.


	The VMAs will take place this year at the Peacock Theatre in Los Angeles, marking the first time the show has been held on the West Coast in nine years. The show was last broadcast from L.A. in 2017, when it was hosted by Katy Perry from the pre-Kia Forum.

	Snoop Dogg is set to host the event, and additional performers, presenters and special guests will be revealed over the next week. The VMAs will air live on September 27 at 4:30 p.m. PT on CBS and will be simulcast on MTV and stream on Paramount+ (Premium) in the United States. It will be available globally the next day on Paramount+ and MTV.

schema.headline: Madonna to Open MTV Video Music Awards With First Show Performance in 23 Years

title: ‘SNL’ Adds New Cast Members Grace Reiter and Saidah Belo-Osagie, Completing Season 52 Ensemble
description:
“Saturday Night Live” has added its first new cast members to Season 52.

	Grace Reiter and Saidah Belo-Osagie are joining the NBC sketch comedy ser
body:
“Saturday Night Live” has added its first new cast members to Season 52.

	Grace Reiter and Saidah Belo-Osagie are joining the NBC sketch comedy series, which returns on Sept. 26 with host Jalen Brunson.

	This is the final “SNL” casting announcement of the season, Variety has learned, with all remaining members of the Season 51 cast returning for Season 52. Of course, that does not include Chloe Fineman, who announced her departure in July, or Bowen Yang, who left mid-season in December. Variety also reported that Martin Herlihy of Please Don’t Destroy is leaving his post as a writer.
	

	Reiter is a Wisconsin-born stand-up comedian and actor who amassed a large following on TikTok and YouTube before she went on to star in Tim Robinson’s HBO comedy series “The Chair Company.” She’s also a member of American High’s sketch team and stars in the upcoming series “Minimum Wage.” Earlier this year, she was listed as one of Variety‘s 10 Creators to Watch.


	Belo-Osagie is a Nigerian American filmmaker and comedian from Queens, who is now based in Brooklyn. She is the creator of the event series Afrobeats Futura and the solo show “Saidah Gets Closure.” In 2020 she wrote and directed a short film called “Tinge.”

	It was reported earlier this summer that both Reiter and Belo-Osagie participated in auditions that took place across Los Angeles, New York and Chicago, where “SNL” executives evaluated more than a dozen comedians.

	The casting announcement comes later than usual for “SNL,” which typically solidifies its troupe in early September.

	With Reiter and Belo-Osagie new to the show, the Season 52 cast is complete. All Season 51 freshmen — Ben Marshall, Tommy Brennan, Jeremy Culhane, Kam Patterson and Veronika Slowikowska — are back, as well as veterans Kenan Thompson, Michael Che, Colin Jost and Mikey Day. Also returning are Andrew Dismukes, Marcello Hernández, James Austin Johnson, Sarah Sherman, Ashley Padilla and Jane Wickline.
	

	“Saturday Night Live” returns to NBC on Sept. 26 with Brunson and musical guest Katseye. The next episodes are headlined by Dakota Johnson and Turnstile on Oct. 3, Shane Gillis and Rosalía on Oct. 10 and Inde Navarette and Gracie Abrams on Oct. 31.

schema.headline: ‘SNL’ Adds New Cast Members Grace Reiter and Saidah Belo-Osagie, Completing Season 52 Ensemble

title: ‘Growth of the Soil’ Review: Norway’s Oscar Entry Is a Robustly Classical, Weatherbeaten Rural Epic
description: The wind deserves above-the-title billing in “Growth of the Soil” — even in the most serene scenes of Hans Petter Moland‘s muscular period epic, you
body:
The wind deserves above-the-title billing in “Growth of the Soil” — even in the most serene scenes of Hans Petter Moland‘s muscular period epic, you can hear it rattling and wheezing and moaning away in the background, or at the very least, you think you can. The elements are crucial characters in this saga of a naïve young couple building a homestead from the ground up in early 20th-century Norway, especially at the outset, where there’s nothing to separate our human protagonists from their battering impact; before they can live off the land, they must live on the land, and surviving it is no guarantee. But it’s not long before this wild, unyielding country is harnessed by progress and gentrification: In the sturdy, sweeping mold of films like “The Emigrants,” “Growth of the Soil” charts the growth of a people via that of a household.
	

	Stately and pleasingly old-fashioned, “Growth of the Soil” plays to the strengths of Moland, a reliable, unflashy journeyman best known internationally for his various collaborations with Stellan Skarsgård, among them the thriller “In Order of Disappearance” (which he remade, with Liam Neeson, as “Cold Pursuit”) and, more pertinently, “Out Stealing Horses,” another decades-spanning literary with a stirring romantic heft to it. (Like that film, Moland’s latest has been selected as Norway’s international Oscar submission.) Minus a crossover star on the level of Skarsgård, this Toronto premiere might not travel as widely as those films, but it should benefit from the rising international profile of its charismatic leading man Herbert Nordrum, the “Worst Person in the World” breakout soon to be seen in English-language productions “Sense and Sensibility” and “Everybody Wants to Fuck Me.”
	

	It was in the excellent but underseen 2023 black comedy “The Hypnosis” that Nordrum really showed his capabilities, winning Best Actor at the Karlovy Vary fest for his flustered but tightly controlled performance as one half of a flailing couple at a startup convention. That film rode on his agitated comic chemistry with Swedish actress Asta Kamma August, so it’s an inspired move to reteam them as lovers with far more visceral problems to deal with in “Growth of the Soil.” This film may bind them together with a shared burden of tragedy, but the actors are once more closely, urgently keyed into each other.

	Isak (Nordrum) and Inger (August) meet as strangers mutually wandering the harsh mountainscapes of untamed northern Norway, swiftly bonding for warmth and companionship as the bitter snowfall comes. We learn little of their respective pasts, while for both, the future is a blank slate: If fate has lumped them together, then they’re not going to argue with that. Isak is stoic and practical, seeking to carve himself a place in this still-unclaimed land; Inger, whose cleft palate has left her feeling alienated from the outside world, finally feels accepted enough to carve it with him. As we cycle through the seasons, their setup evolves from a temporary structure to a handbuilt stone house to a thriving farm shared with their two strapping sons.

	As a peripheral community grows around them, this lawless terrain is suddenly subject to boundaries and contracts and taxes; both uneducated and illiterate, Isak and Inger are ill prepared for such societal evolution. But their primitive way of living reveals itself to rather more devastating effect when their third child is born, and Inger commits an act of unthinkable desperation. From this point on, the couple’s devoted, almost hermetically sealed-off life together is irretrievably shattered, and the outside world intrudes in ways both progressive and ruinous.

	Co-written by Moland and Gard B. Eidsvold, “Growth of the Soil” is adapted from a two-volume 1917 novel by Nobel laureate Knut Hamsun, and the film honors that literary formality and sweep. At a very full 155 minutes, it’s stately but engrossing, enlivened by the detailed, slow-burning interior transformations unfolding in both lead performances — not to mention some vital external changes too. 
	

	It’s an interesting side note that August is the daughter of “Pelle the Conqueror” director Bille; “Growth of the Soil” feels like the kind of film he might have made in his heyday, when such rustic arthouse epics were bigger business. Shot with rugged austerity rather than overly pictorial prettiness by Oskar Dahlsbakken, with that scratching, howling sound design at least as prominent as the musical score, this is a slightly more sober version of those, but transportive nonetheless.

schema.headline: ‘Growth of the Soil’ Review: Norway’s Oscar Entry Is a Robustly Classical, Weatherbeaten Rural Epic

title: Matthew Lillard Says ‘I Feel Ashamed’ for Acting in ‘Scream 7’ After Melissa Barrera Got Fired: ‘I Blew That. I’m on the Wrong Side of History’
description: Matthew Lillard feels “ashamed” for starring in this year’s “Scream 7” after Melissa Barrera was fired from the franchise due to social media posts
body:
Matthew Lillard feels “ashamed” for starring in this year’s “Scream 7” after Melissa Barrera was fired from the franchise due to social media posts criticizing Israel amid the war in Gaza. Lillard starred in Wes Craven’s original “Scream” in 1996 as Stu Macher. He reprised the role in “Scream 7,” which opened in theaters in February and became the highest-grossing entry in the series with $214 million.

	Attending a recent 30th anniversary screening of the original “Scream,” Lillard was asked by a fan about the difficulty of speaking out on politics as an actor. Lillard made headlines last year for saying “fuck ICE” at a “Scream” screening.
	

	“I don’t know how else to do it,” Lillard told the fan (via Entertainment Weekly). “For me, I have queer kids. If I’m not standing up for queer kids or kids in the trans community, then what the fuck am I doing? If I’m not standing up against ICE, then what the fuck am I doing?”


	Lillard noted that “I don’t think it’s easy all the time” to speak out, noting what happened to Barrera as an example. “Scream” franchise producer Spyglass fired her after she starred in two franchise installments and was gearing up to return for “Scream 7.” The company said it had “zero tolerance for antisemitism or the incitement of hate in any form, including false references to genocide, ethnic cleansing, Holocaust distortion or anything that flagrantly crosses the line into hate speech.”

	“Melissa Barrera, who’s a beautiful actor, was fired for what she said after the whole Palestinian — what started happening in Israel,” Lillard said. “It’s really fucking bullshit and really hard, and she’s on the right side of history. When they start coming after your job, sometimes things are worth it… When that happened to Melissa, the whole world didn’t pipe up. But she was a year early on what the fuck’s going on. But the whole world should have popped up and said, ‘She’s right.’ And they didn’t. And that’s brutal.”
	

	“I went back to do ‘Scream,’ and I got called out. And I’m like, ‘Oh, fuck. That’s brutal,’” he continued. “I feel bad about that. I feel ashamed about that. Because in that moment I was so excited to go back, I didn’t really think about Melissa and that journey. I didn’t say no. I’m embarrassed; that’s the truth… I blew that. I’m on the wrong side of history for that. I still like being in the movie [but] it may not have been the best idea.”

	After war broke out in Gaza in 2023, Barrera took to Instagram to share her views on the conflict. She was critical of Israel and accused the nation of “genocide and ethnic cleansing.” The post led to her firing, which in turn sparked backlash from her supporters against the release of “Scream 7”. Protesters gathered outside of the “Scream 7” premiere in Los Angeles, for instance, and called for a boycott of the horror film in a show of support for Palestine.

schema.headline: Matthew Lillard Says ‘I Feel Ashamed’ for Acting in ‘Scream 7’ After Melissa Barrera Got Fired: ‘I Blew That. I’m on the Wrong Side of History’

title: Box Office: ‘Resident Evil’ Reboot Targets Franchise-Best $45 Million Debut
description:
Movie theater operators are counting on “Resident Evil” to scare some life into the early fall box office. 

	Sony’s horror-comedy reboot of the zom
body:
Movie theater operators are counting on “Resident Evil” to scare some life into the early fall box office. 

	Sony’s horror-comedy reboot of the zombie-infested property is targeting a strong $40 million to $50 million in its domestic debut. With strong reviews and glowing word-of-mouth, rivals and independent tracking services believe that initial ticket sales will surpass $50 million and could near $60 million.


	Sony spent $75 million to produce the movie, the second remake and eighth installment in the horror series. Exhibitors are particularly excited because this take on “Resident Evil” was directed by Zach Cregger, who electrified the box office with last August’s breakout hit “Weapons.” That R-rated movie, an original thriller about students who went missing in the middle of the night, opened to $43 million en route to sleeper hit status. “Weapons” ended its box office run with a mighty $270 million globally against a $38 million budget and won an Oscar for Amy Madigan. 
	

	“Resident Evil” began as a 1996 video game and expanded into a multimedia franchise that spans sequel games and film and television adaptations. The property was first adapted for the big screen in 2002’s “Resident Evil,” starring Milla Jovovich. She reprised her role as Alice, a former security specialist and covert operative, in five follow-up films in the 2000s and 2010s. Those movies collectively generated $1 billion globally and were once the highest-grossing series based on video games. Sony attempted to reboot the property with 2021’s “Resident Evil: Welcome to Raccoon City,” a critical and commercial failure with $42 million worldwide against a $25 million budget. All of the original “Resident Evil” films opened in the $20 million range (not adjusted for inflation), while “Welcome to Raccoon City” faltered with $5.3 million in its debut, so this reboot will easily rank as the largest opening weekend in the long-running franchise. The highest grossing installment is 2010’s “Resident Evil: Afterlife,” which launched to $26 million domestically and ended its theatrical run with $300 million globally.
	

	In the new “Resident Evil,” Cregger reunites with “Weapons” actor Austin Abrams, who stars as a medical courier who fights through a viral outbreak of infested monsters in Raccoon City. Critics have praised the cinematic gorefest, with Variety’s Owen Gleiberman calling it “different, and much better, than the other ‘Resident Evil’ movies.”

	As this weekend’s only major release, “Resident Evil” won’t have any trouble securing the No. 1 spot on domestic box office charts. Elsewhere, “Practical Magic 2” will attempt to rebound after a rough start while mid-summer holdovers like “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “The Odyssey” will remain atop box office charts. 

	Although this weekend is light on newcomers, the fall box office is expected to heat up before September ends. Next weekend brings a trio of new movies, including Paramount’s Brad Pitt-led survival thriller “Heart of the Beast,” Universal and DreamWorks Animation’s “Forgotten Island” and A24’s “To Catch a Predator”-inspired “Primetime,” starring Robert Pattinson. There’s also Disney’s re-release of “Avengers: Endgame,” which is returning to theaters before “Avengers: Doomsday” opens in December. In the meantime, it’s Cregger and his band of zombie slayers to the rescue.

schema.headline: Box Office: ‘Resident Evil’ Reboot Targets Franchise-Best $45 Million Debut

            Internal discussions in the Los Angeles Mayor's Office and the California Attorney General's Office were told Paramount would announce it was leaving California, but there's a twist ... sources tell TMZ.
      
    
            We're told the Mayor and the A.G. were told the announcement would come yesterday, but it did not happen. We do not know if circumstances changed or if there was just a delay.
      
    
            As you probably know, the California Attorney General -- other with 11 other state attorneys general -- have filed an anti-trust lawsuit against Paramount, trying to block the Warner Bros merger.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            David Ellison, the CEO of Paramount, has threatened to move the studio to Texas, Tennessee or Georgia if the Cali A.G. didn't back off and settle.
      
    
            There were settlement negotiations over the last few months, but they couldn't reach a deal. Attorney General Rob Bonta said Paramount was being unreasonable.
      
    
            Ellison threatened to leave California if a settlement wasn't reached by October 1st. Based on conversations in both the Mayor's and Attorney General's offices ... it sounds like no deal is possible.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            If Paramount pulls the trigger, it will be a devastating 1-2 punch for Hollywood. "American Idol" is leaving Hollywood for Atlanta. Many other productions have also left Hollywood over the last few years. Fact is ... if Hollywood isn't dead, it's dying.
      
    
            We reached out to Paramount ... they said "no comment."

title: Michael Jackson Estate Fighting Daughter Paris' Demand for $1 Million in Legal Fees
description:

                          Beat It, Paris ...

body:
Michael Jackson Estate
                          Beat It, Paris ...
                          $1 Million in Legal Fees Is Way Too Much
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 16, 2026
                            2:10 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Michael Jackson's estate is responding to Paris Jackson's request for over $1 million in legal fees ... and they think she won't stop 'til she gets too much!
      
    
            The executor of Michael's estate, John Branca, filed legal docs objecting to Paris' request Monday ... claiming her ask for the estate to fork over $1,165,481.90 in legal bills just isn't reasonable.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we've reported ... Paris disputed $625,000 in bonuses paid to attorneys of her late father's estate back in 2018 ... and the court sided with her in April of this year, ordering the money to be returned to the estate.
      

            Because Paris was able to secure the dough for the benefit of the estate, the judge ruled the estate had to pay her "reasonable" legal fees in securing the benefit ... and Paris requested a whopping $1.16 million.
      
    
            Now, the estate is arguing these fees are way too high, insisting she is trying to collect fees for unrelated legal battles in the case and claiming she is exaggerating how much she actually saved the estate, noting that some of the money she's counting was actually voluntarily returned to the estate.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The bottom line ... Branca is fine with Paris getting paid, just for the fights he says she won and for the benefits she actually got for the estate's beneficiaries.
      
    
            We'll keep you posted on how this legal thriller turns out.
